paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: A Plinian eruption is a volcanic eruption that resembles the one at Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD. That eruption destroyed the ancient Roman cities of Herculaneum and Pompeii, and it is the prototype for the whole type. Another name for the type is Vesuvian eruption. Pliny the Younger described the 79 AD event in a letter, written after his uncle, Pliny the Elder, had died.

paragraphs.heading: How it behaves
paragraphs.text: These eruptions throw columns of volcanic debris and hot gas high into the stratosphere, which is the second layer of Earth's atmosphere. The blast is powerful, continuous and driven by gas, and it throws out a large amount of pumice. Some eruptions are over in less than a day. Others go on for days or months, and the longer ones start by producing clouds of volcanic ash, sometimes along with pyroclastic surges.

paragraphs.heading: What is left behind
paragraphs.text: So much magma can be thrown out that the magma chamber below is depleted. The top of the volcano then collapses, and the result is a caldera. Fine ash and pulverized pumice can settle over large areas.

paragraphs.heading: Sound and lightning
paragraphs.text: Loud sounds often go with a Plinian eruption. Lightning is common too. Electrical charge builds up in the air around the rising column of ash, and when it suddenly discharges, lightning strikes. The English geologist George Julius Poulett Scrope showed this in a painting of 1822, and the same thing was seen in 2022 when Hunga-Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai erupted.

paragraphs.heading: The kind of lava
paragraphs.text: The lava is usually dacitic or rhyolitic, and rich in silica. Basaltic lava, which is low in silica, rarely produces a Plinian eruption. It needs specific conditions: magma water content below 2%, moderate temperature and rapid crystallization. A recent basaltic case is Mount Tarawera, on the North Island of New Zealand, which erupted in 1886.

paragraphs.heading: The death of Pliny the Elder
paragraphs.text: Pliny the Elder set out to rescue people from a dangerous position on the shore of the Bay of Naples. He launched his galleys and crossed the bay to Stabiae. His nephew described the death and suggested that the older man collapsed and died after breathing poisonous gases from the volcano. The body was found on 26 August, buried under the ash with no apparent injuries, after the plume had cleared. That fits asphyxiation or poisoning, but it fits a heart attack, an asthma attack or a stroke as well.

paragraphs.heading: Ultra-Plinian eruptions
paragraphs.text: In 1980 the volcanologist George P. Walker proposed a new class, ultra-Plinian, with the Hatepe eruption as its representative. He based it on that eruption's exceptional dispersive power and the height of its column. The threshold is an eruptive column 45 km high, or 41 km more recently. On the Volcanic Explosivity Index, an ultra-Plinian eruption would be at least VEI-5. The Hatepe case has since been called into question: recent evidence points to an unrecognized shift in the wind field, not extreme eruptive vigor.
